O.outcome_detail: perceived value and positive experience of the training

result.effect: 24/28 positive responses; 4/28 needed more time to assess impact

cells.note: The study did not include a no-training comparison group; the comparison is between qualitative response categories within the post-programme sample.

O.outcome_detail: self-value, empowerment, self-confidence and job perceptions

cells.quote: Of the 14 participants who were able to implement their training upon returning to practice, the majority expressed feelings of increased self‐value, empowerment and self‐confidence (93%; 13/14): ‘I have felt empowered that I have been able to provide a more positive experience for people and their pets’, and ‘I have gained a new‐found sense of confidence in myself. As well as see[ing] how valuable I am to myself’. Some of these same participants (29%; 4/14) described their job as being more exciting because of being given the chance to work with clients and to use their communication skills: ‘The difficult conversations are much less intimidating now! I am excited to work with clients more and more’.
cells.note: This was a manifest content analysis of 2-month follow-up open-ended responses. The comparison is qualitative: participants unable to implement the training often expressed less-favourable job views, while those able to implement it reported more positive views.

O.outcome_detail: predictive cue effects on subjective pain

cells.quote: Predictive cues dynamically modulated pain perception as contingencies changed, regardless of whether participants received contingency instructions.
cells.note: The study describes similar cue effects across groups, but does not report an equivalence test; therefore this is inconclusive rather than evidence of no difference.

result.effect: NPS and SIIPS group differences: p>0.2

cells.quote: We also observed robust expression of both the Neurologic Signature Pattern (NPS; Wager et al., 2013) and Stimulus-Intensity Independent Pain Signature (SIIPS; Woo et al., 2017) as a function of temperature-related changes in both groups (all p’s<0.001, see Table 2) and signature pattern expression did not differ by group (all p’s>0.2; see Figure 2C&D and Table 2).
cells.note: This cell concerns pain-related signature responses; the study also reported some group differences in specific regions, including the left hippocampus and right primary somatosensory cortex.

result.effect: Right striatum: b=0.24, p=0.03; expected value shaped by instructions versus error-based updating

cells.quote: Quantitative modeling revealed that expected value was shaped purely by instructions in the Instructed Group, whereas expected value updated dynamically in the Uninstructed Group as a function of error-based learning.
cells.note: The groups used different computational mechanisms; this is a dissociation, not a better-versus-worse learning result.

O.outcome_detail: brain response in the rostroventral medulla across reversals

cells.quote: Heat-evoked responses in the insula, anterior cingulate, and other regions updated as contingencies changed, and responses in the prefrontal cortex mediated dynamic cue effects on pain, whereas responses in the brainstem’s rostroventral medulla (RVM) were shaped by initial contingencies throughout the task.
cells.note: This codes the entry's finding about brain responses retaining sensitivity to initial/original contingencies.
